extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political communication, journalists, historians, and policymakers interested in public opinion and persuasion
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how public leaders, parties, and organizers craft phrases, symbols, and organizational choices to mobilize mass opinion and present clear choices (e.g., how the Fourteen Points were formulated and used). Emphasizes messenger credibility, timing, phrasing, organizational structure, and the necessary simplicity of mass decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no power in the symbol except that which it acquires by association in the human mind; symbols that have lost their power or never take root show a secular history of circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose symbols that resonate with the audience's experience and imagination. Recognize that vacant, general phrases (e.g., 'Rights of Humanity') can evoke strong emotion but little concrete meaning; museums and folklore hold many 'dead emblems' as warnings. Examples: the Fourteen Points, Hamilton's national symbols; monitor whether a symbol is actually rooted in constituents' experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of the messenger
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols are planted in people's minds by other human beings whom they recognize as authoritative; symbols become important when introduced by congenial and important people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize credible, trusted messengers (parents, teachers, leaders, editors) when introducing an idea. Where facts are out of sight, people choose between trustworthy and untrustworthy reporters rather than between truth and falsehood. Use authorities that the target audience already respects to seed symbolic meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and strategic placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols must be employed by somebody at a particular moment; they must be spoken by people who are strategically placed, and they must be spoken at the opportune moment—otherwise they are mere wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the moment and the venue for releasing a symbol or phrase. A strategically timed statement (e.g., the Fourteen Points when morale and attention were poised) can crystallize disparate opinions; ill-timed symbols fail even if well chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of mass choices (Yes or No)
rubrics_metrics.description: The limit of direct action is for all practical purposes the power to say Yes or No on an issue presented to the mass; mass decisions almost always require a simple, concrete choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking mass action or votes, frame issues into clear, simple choices (binary or strongly prioritized alternatives). Even mechanisms like referenda or preferential ballots ultimately depend on the quality and clarity of the choices presented. Avoid overly complex or subtle measures if the aim is broad public decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and role of the organizing 'machine' or hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass cooperation in complex affairs requires a central machine managed by a very few people; in any institution the number who govern is a very small percentage of those who are supposed to govern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge and utilize organizational hierarchies (caucus, nominating convention, steering committee) to formulate and present choices. Machines transmit coordinated symbols and convert private motives into collective action; attempts to eliminate the machine (e.g., pure direct democracy) do not remove the need for leadership that presents decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful, calculated phrasing to cover contingencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Wording must be meticulously chosen to condense a complex set of interests in a few words and to cover multiple contingencies (e.g., the Fourteen Points choice of 'righted' instead of 'restored' for Alsace-Lorraine; use of 'Prussia' and the date '1871').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft phrases that can satisfy different constituencies without committing to outcomes that would fracture allied support. Use wording to signal specific meanings to informed audiences while preserving plausible deniability or flexibility for broader publics. Numbering and formal presentation (e.g., enumerating points) can create an impression of precision and businesslike intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between generalization and particularity
rubrics_metrics.description: As appeals ascend the hierarchy of symbols (to include more factions) they become more generalized and lose intellectual content; high-level phrases stir emotion but disperse meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the objective is to unify many groups, general symbols may be effective emotionally, but to convert sentiment into concrete policy or sustained action, anchor messages with particular, experience-based content. Be aware that very general slogans will be interpreted differently by different groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a competing narrative or alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Public statements should offer a genuine alternative to rival narratives (e.g., the Fourteen Points were intended as an alternative to Brest-Litovsk negotiations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure messaging not only asserts ideals but also competes with and undercuts opposing frames. Presenting an alternative spectacle or public debate can draw attention away from rival solutions and redirect popular sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate hidden commitments and reconcile public language
rubrics_metrics.description: Allied governments were bound by engagements and secret treaties which conflicted with public conceptions; public declarations must be formulated with awareness of these hidden commitments and of what constituencies remember (e.g., invoking '1871').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for prior secret agreements, official obligations, and popular memories when framing public statements. Use historical references and carefully chosen specifics to redefine contested boundaries or to cast aside inconvenient secret terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associate symbols with deep constituent attachments
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols that are deeply attached (e.g., 'France') have stronger hold than recent or omnibus symbols (e.g., 'Europe'); political language should preserve those symbols that have permanent roots in the imagination of constituents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor appeals to symbols already embedded in the audience's lived experience and loyalties. Where possible, translate broader ideals into nationally or locally resonant symbols so that symbolic appeals can sustain political unity and mobilization.
